opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so when AlphaFold 3 came out, it was a big step forward. Going beyond single protein chains to model complexes with ligands, nucleic acids, modifications, all in one framework was a big deal for anyone working on drug discovery. But at release, the community couldn't really get their hands on it. There was a web server with restrictions, and no code or weights at first. So a lot of people, especially in industry, couldn't use it for the things they actually cared about, like running it on proprietary molecules or folding it into their own pipelines.

For us at Chai, the question was really: what do we need for our own work? We're trying to build a platform for molecular design, and structure prediction is a foundational piece of that. We needed a model we understood end to end, could modify, could condition on extra information, and could build on. So we were going to build one regardless.

Once we had something that matched or got close to that level of performance, releasing it openly felt like the obvious move. It gave researchers and companies something they could actually use, including commercially, and it built goodwill and credibility with the community we want to work with. We also saw a gap that open models could fill. We added things like support for embeddings from protein language models, so you could run it without MSAs, and the ability to bring in experimental restraints. Those are the practical knobs people want in real discovery settings.

There's also a scientific argument. This field moves fastest when people can reproduce, probe, and break models. AlphaFold 2 being open is a big reason the ecosystem around it exploded. We wanted to help keep that dynamic going, rather than have the best structure prediction tools sit behind closed doors. Honestly, structure prediction is becoming table stakes. The real differentiation is in what you build on top of it, so opening up that layer cost us relatively little and gave a lot back.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Chai needed a model it could understand and build on for its platform, and that it planned to build one regardless. It does not identify building the open model as a forcing function for developing the infrastructure Chai needed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there were a few things going on at once. When AlphaFold 3 came out, the paper was there, but the weights and the code weren't, and even once the code eventually came out it was under a license that made it hard to use for anything commercial. So you had this huge step forward in the field, and at the same time most of the people who actually wanted to build on it, biotechs, pharma, academic labs doing drug discovery, couldn't really touch it. That felt like a gap worth filling.

The second thing is that we were going to build this model anyway. Chai's whole thesis is that we want to do structure prediction and molecular design at the frontier, and you can't do that by sitting on top of someone else's closed model. So the question was never "should we train it," it was "should we release it." And releasing it is a pretty cheap decision once you've already paid for the training run. You give up some moat, but honestly, I don't think a single model release is the moat. The moat is the team, the data, the iteration speed, the stuff you build on top.

And then there's the practical side. If you release openly, people find your bugs. They tell you which targets you're bad at, they try it on antibodies and nucleic acids and weird covalent ligands that we didn't have time to stress test ourselves. That feedback loop is enormously valuable, and you just don't get it if the model lives behind an API that only a handful of people use. For a small company, that's basically free red-teaming and free benchmarking.

I'd also say there was a bit of a community argument. Structure prediction got to where it is because of CASP, because of the PDB, because people shared things. AlphaFold 2 being open is a big part of why the whole field moved so fast after 2021. It seemed like the right thing to do to keep that going rather than have the field fracture into a bunch of closed, slightly different versions of the same architecture.

And finally, from a pure positioning standpoint, we were a new lab nobody had heard of. Putting out something that was competitive with AlphaFold 3, with the weights available, was the fastest way to show people we were serious and get good people to want to work with us. So it was partly principled and partly pretty pragmatic.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Chai planned to build the model to pursue frontier work, but does not identify building an open-source model as a forcing function to develop needed infrastructure.

astra-6.text:
AlphaFold 3 was a big validation that this approach could work, but a paper and a model you can actually build on are different things. We thought there was a lot of value in making that capability openly available, so people could run it themselves, experiment with it, and integrate it into their own research.

And we didn’t think the problem was solved. Predicting a structure is an important piece, but there’s still a lot to do to make these models useful for discovering drugs. For us, building an open model was a way to establish that foundation and give the community something useful while we continued pushing the technology forward.

r001.rationale: The response says an open model would make the capability available to the community and establish a foundation, but it does not identify building it as a forcing function for Chai to develop needed infrastructure.

sol-6.1.text:
For us, AlphaFold 3 was a strong validation of the direction we were already pursuing. But a paper showing what’s possible isn’t the same as giving people a model they can actually build on. If you want to develop new methods, run predictions at scale, or integrate structure prediction into a drug discovery workflow, access and flexibility really matter.

So we thought there was still a lot of value in building an openly available model that people could run themselves and experiment with. And the problem isn’t solved just because one very good model exists. There’s room to improve accuracy, understand where these systems fail, and make them more useful for designing molecules. That’s very aligned with what we want to do at Chai.

r001.rationale: The response says an open model would let people run predictions and experiment, but it does not identify building the model as a forcing function for Chai to develop needed infrastructure.
